column6: Scope note: the MLX stack moves weekly; pin versions or every dated claim in this part may have drifted.
Six core-MLX traps where numbers go quietly wrong: scalar cache keys, frozen captured arrays, invisible NumPy mutations.
M5 float32 matmul silently runs at TF32-class precision (2^-10.4 vs 2^-19.8 error); set MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0 before import.
Affine gather_qmm on M5 leaves output rows unwritten (mlx#3856); they read back whatever the recycled MTLBuffer held.
mlx-lm applies a chat template you didn't pick, and --use-default-chat-template is a no-op in generate; six traps total.
The server returns HTTP 404 for model-load, OOM and tokenizer failures, and tools to a non-tool model only warns.
Adapters train under a chat template serving may not reproduce (enable_thinking auto-defaults); quality quietly shifts.
Scope note: signatures below are verified against source and docs; check the evidence ladder before trusting.
MLX_ENABLE_TF32 is read on first use - set after your first matmul it silently does nothing; matvec shapes stay fp32.
The mx.metal.* memory spellings are deprecated and print to stderr on first call; use the top-level equivalents.
mlx_lm.load's default lazy=False evaluates every parameter at load - an 18.2 GB spike on a 35B MoE before any token.
A loop that never calls mx.eval builds an ever-growing lazy graph; memory climbs until evaluation or OOM.
Lazy evaluation moves exceptions to whatever line forces evaluation, far from the op that caused them.
A failing op raises nothing when recorded; the exception fires at a later print or eval, often inside a library.
Evaluating loss and gradients separately runs the graph twice per step; batch both into one mx.eval.
Community-measured functional-cache leak: memory grows across steps until the cache is explicitly cleared.
custom_function silently zeroes gradients for arrays captured by closure.
Arrays captured by custom_function become constants; their gradients are silently 0.0 and training never updates them.
The first compiled call pays graph build, codegen and Metal compilation; un-warmed benchmarks measure the compiler.
Arrays captured by an mx.compile closure freeze at trace time; later updates never reach the compiled function.
state[0] = new value has no effect on a compiled function that captured it; it keeps returning the traced constant.
A varying Python scalar argument recompiles a compiled function on every call; it presents as compile being slower.
int/float/str/None args are baked into the compile cache key; a varying scalar silently recompiles every call.
shapeless=True only exempts shape changes; scalar constants varying across calls still create distinct cache entries.
Under shapeless=True, Python arithmetic on x.shape freezes at trace time and later shapes compute with stale values.
shapeless compile bakes shape-derived arithmetic from the first call; new shapes silently reuse the frozen numbers.
The default-stream context manager is part of the compile cache key; calling under another device recompiles.
A stream is only usable on its creating thread; workers get 'There is no Stream(gpu, 0) in current thread'.
Per-call stream setup costs a uniform 55-77 ms TTFT regression (mlx-lm#1435); hoist it out of the hot path.
The applegpu g/s suffix-to-product mapping is disputed between MLX source and community; don't identify products by it.
A NumPy array or float on self is not a parameter - never saved or restored - and underscore names are invisible too.
cross_entropy's reduction defaults to 'none' and accepted literals are unverified; omit it and average yourself.
apply(astype) casts packed uint32 quantized weights and integer params to bfloat16, destroying them; use set_dtype.
load_weights(strict=False) skips shape checks entirely; mismatched weights load and the model silently misbehaves.
mx.load's format list omits gguf, and unsupported GGUF quantization formats silently cast tensors to another dtype.
mx.save forces evaluation of the pending graph; a checkpoint line can trigger the entire deferred computation.
Writing through a NumPy view mutates MLX memory invisibly to autodiff; gradients come back wrong.
External mutation of MLX memory is invisible to autodiff: Apple's own demo returns the wrong gradient with no error.
DLPack hands over a pointer without synchronising; reading in torch before MLX's stream finishes yields wrong values.
export_function is experimental; .mlxfn files from older MLX versions may not load in future ones.
Skip mx.eval before exporting a module and the .mlxfn captures the initialiser - it runs with fresh random weights.
Scope note: verify signatures below against source; the NAX story is new and evidence is mixed.
Three NAX correctness PRs within three days (#3912 quant corruption, #3922 gather_qmm bounds); pin and re-verify.
TOC: precision you did not choose - float32 matmuls at TF32 class with no runtime signal.
TOC: the silent SDPA fallback from fused kernel to unfused matmul-softmax.
complex64 matmul is gated out of the NAX path on Metal, while CUDA gives complex TF32 fast math instead.
np.array on bfloat16 raises a cryptic PEP 3118 error, and NumPy float64 silently narrows to MLX float32.
On M5 + macOS 26.2+, float32 matmul defaults to reduced internal precision with no runtime signal.
M5 float32 matmul returns plausible values ~3 orders of magnitude less accurate; x.dtype still says float32.
The M5 material is a launch Tech Talk, not a WWDC session; weigh its numbers accordingly.
Do not write a blanket '26.2 required'; Apple's own narrated version ladder skips 26.2 entirely.
A source build targeting below macOS 26.2 defines MLX_METAL_NO_NAX: a working MLX that is simply never fast on M5.
MLX's g/s suffix table and community observation disagree; use the suffix for buffer sizing, never product ID.
Do not use mx.metal.device_info(); the mx.metal.* family is deprecated and forwards with a stderr notice.
Each Apple M5 speedup uses a different baseline; a number without its baseline is meaningless.
Apple's trace shows simdgroup_matrix kernels leave M5 matrix hardware idle; the same matmul is ~7x faster on TensorOps.
Every figure here is Apple-published with hardware and OS unstated beyond 'M5'; don't generalize.
mx.fast SDPA silently takes the unfused path for many configurations; right answer, worse speed and memory.
gpt-oss attention sinks plus a quantized KV cache kill the generation thread; the client sees only a timeout.
Fused SDPA is inference-only on Metal; training deliberately uses the unfused path, which is what benchmarks measure.
SDPA fallback computes correct output unfused, materialising the full score tensor; throughput and memory betray it.
Correction: Gemma 4's global layers are head_dim 512, not 256; a clean A/B showed no change at 32K/64K.
mx.get_peak_memory excludes the buffer pool; one M5 Max run reported 46 GB while the OS saw ~110 GB.
MLX_SDPA_BLOCKS not a multiple of 32 silently corrupts attention every decode step on mlx <=0.32.0 (fixed in PR #3875).
math_mode relaxed/fast stops guaranteeing exp(-inf)==0; masked positions leak into softmax: plausible, wrong attention.
The fused grid-sample speedup is MLX's own published number with hardware unstated; re-measure on your machine.
ensure_row_contiguous=False with raw linear indexing reads strided buffers wrong: right shape, wrong contents, no error.
Custom-kernel outputs are uninitialized by default; without init_value, unwritten slots hold recycled buffer contents.
A kernel weight captured by closure gets no gradient under custom_function; pass tensors as arguments instead.
Overview: four quantized-matmul corruption defects with issue numbers, most reproducible only on M5-generation hardware.
Scope note: quantization numbers below carry mixed provenance; check each one's sourcing before quoting.
TOC: the register of quantized-matmul corruption bugs.
MLX's fp8_e8m0, fp8_e4m3 and fp4_e2m1 are its own structs, not interchangeable with other stacks' formats.
Layers whose input dim doesn't divide the group size are silently left in full precision.
A Linear not divisible by group_size is silently kept full-precision: your 4-bit model is 4-bit except awkward layers.
Miss a NAX dispatch gate and you get correct numbers from a much slower kernel, with nothing logged.
Shapes failing the K%64/transpose check dispatch a non-NAX kernel: no warning, same numbers, very different M5 speed.
The routed-only read numbers are community-measured (john-rocky, partly agent-generated repo), not Apple-published.
DWQ on mxfp4/mxfp8/nvfp4 or 8-bit affine runs, prints losses, and writes a checkpoint quantized identically to input.
Seven quantized-matmul defects, five exclusive to M5-generation hardware; the register with statuses.
gather_qmm's unwritten rows aren't zeros: they hold recycled MTLBuffer contents, sometimes coincidentally plausible.
Decision-table flag: M5 MoE with affine 4-bit sits on two open corruption bugs; pad gathered rows to 64, keep K%64==0.
mlx-lm 0.31.0 was pulled from PyPI for BatchKV cache cross-contamination; know exactly which version you run.
rich and regex are imported at module level but undeclared; a bare pip install crashes at import.
Scope note: flag names below were verified against argparse declarations, not the docs.
Marker for this guide's register of six silent failures; none of them throw.
DEFAULT_XTC_THRESHOLD is 0.0 but the CLI default for --xtc-threshold is 0.1 - one of four disagreeing XTC defaults.
--use-default-chat-template is accepted by mlx_lm.generate and does nothing.
LEARNED_QUANTS.md's DWQ and AWQ defaults don't match the code (1024/8 vs 2048/4; 32/10 vs 128/20); trust --help.
--draft-model silently disables continuous batching; concurrent requests serialize.
--prefill-step-size doubles as the quantized-KV memory knob; tuning one silently changes the other.
LORA.md says to pass --hf-path to mlx_lm.fuse, but the flag doesn't exist; GGUF export covers only three model types.
mlx_lm.benchmark empties the tokenizer's EOS set in place; reuse that tokenizer and generation never stops.
generate() returns None, not '', when no text is emitted; .strip() callers crash exactly on the worst inputs.
stream_generate(max_tokens=0) raises UnboundLocalError; for prefill-only, call generate_step and drain the generator.
ChunkedKVCache and ConcatenateKVCache break the server prompt cache's trim assumptions; hits can return mismatched KV.
load_prompt_cache rebuilds classes from mlx_lm.models.cache globals; a custom cache class saves but cannot load back.
--kv-bits starts cleanly, /health answers 200, then the first request crashes on sliding-window models (mlx-lm#1573).
Quantized KV with gpt-oss kills the generation thread; the request never returns and presents as a network timeout.
The CLI hard-errors on draft/model tokenizer mismatch; the server only warns and proceeds with speculative decoding.
An unregistered drafter makes the Swift MTP iterator fall back to single-token decoding: no error, zero speedup.
BatchGenerator.insert writes new caches into the very list you passed; held references mutate under you.
A draft model or a seed silently turns the concurrent server sequential; concurrency holds only when batchable.
mlx-lm applies a chat template in cases where you expected yours or none; --use-default-chat-template is a no-op.
Quantized-KV settings change output quality through three separate mechanisms, with no signal.
Several sampler parameters are accepted and never reach the sampler; outputs don't change.
stream_generate silently drops unknown kwargs; a typoed sampler argument changes nothing and raises nothing.
The server's prompt-cache reuse can return KV that doesn't match your tokens, mixing another prompt's context in.
The Swift port carries its own KV-cache bugs; Mac apps hit them through cache reuse.
Scope note: server signatures verified from source at a pinned commit; PyPI lags main by months.
The server imports undeclared packages at module level; a clean install crashes before serving anything.
--allowed-origins defaults to the string '*', making origin checks substring tests; pass it explicitly for a real list.
/health is a static handler; it answers 200 regardless of whether the model loaded or the generation thread is alive.
Model-load, OOM and tokenizer failures return HTTP 404 - the mistyped-URL status; the real error hides in the body.
tools passed to a model that can't call tools only logs a warning; the response just never contains tool calls.
A draft model or a fixed seed silently disables continuous batching; the server serves sequentially.
Cache classes that aren't trimmable forfeit prompt-prefix reuse entirely; every turn pays a full prefill.
Freshness: NAX code paths are new and moving, with three correctness fixes within days of writing.
--host 0.0.0.0 exposes a server with no authentication; anyone on the network can drive your model.
HTTP exposes no logits, so @Generable guided generation is unavailable on this path; use tools plus your own validation.
ChatCompletionsLanguageModel's literal 'v1' check appends /v1/chat/completions after non-/v1 base paths, producing 404s.
macOS 26.2 is the hard gate for RDMA-over-Thunderbolt distributed inference; older machines simply can't join.
The first successful distributed init wins: later init() or backend='any' calls return the first backend, not a new one.
Ring backend restriction: send and recv work only between ring neighbours, not arbitrary ranks.
The two best sources give different RDMA setup sequences; both are quoted - pick one deliberately.
Dict hostfile entries are read with data['backend'] not .get(); omit the key and the launcher raises KeyError.
--output does not exist on the launcher; the real flag is --output-hostfile.
Distributed runs need MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1; without it, CPU-driven communication pays slow GPU-CPU synchronisation.
Counterweight mlx#3830: FAST_SYNCH can deadlock a Metal fence and lock the GPU until reboot; unset, the watchdog fires.
--auto-setup disables the Thunderbolt Bridge on every machine - a destructive network-config change on each node.
Script and model paths resolve on each node, not the launcher; launcher-local paths fail or run stale copies remotely.
The docs' NCCL example passes --no-verify-script, a flag the launcher does not have.
Not all models support pipeline parallelism; check before planning a pipelined topology.
--batch-size is the global batch split across N nodes; leave it unscaled and each node trains on batch/N.
Apple's distributed speedup comes with its own caveat - it depends on setup; quote the caveat with the number.
180 to 600 tok/s are the session's only absolute figures; every other distributed claim is a ratio.
The RDMA port forum report is community-reported with unknown status and no replies captured.
mlx_lm.lora imports two more packages at module scope that setup.py never declares; bare installs crash.
Every file:line cite pins commit e5baded; on any other commit expect line numbers to have drifted.
Python LoRALinear defaults scale=20.0; the Swift stack's default differs, so ported adapters silently change behavior.
rich and regex must be installed by hand; they're imported at module scope but undeclared in setup.py.
On a bare pip install, mlx_lm.lora dies at import: cli_ui pulls rich at module scope (ModuleNotFoundError).
PyPI's mlx-lm (0.31.3, April) trails main by months of fixes; 0.31.0 was yanked for BatchKV cross-contamination.
Training data renders under enable_thinking auto-defaults; serving with another template quietly degrades the adapter.
A missing valid.jsonl only warns: a full run completes with no validation curve and no overfitting signal.
ConcatenatedDataset.__getitem__ writes a _dataset key into the record it returns, mutating your data in place.
--clear-cache-threshold parses fine and is silently ignored; it never reaches the trainer.
--resume-adapter-file loads with strict=False, so misshapen or misnamed weights are silently skipped.
The example config contradicts CONFIG_DEFAULTS; copying it silently changes schedule values.
--clear-cache-threshold never reaches the trainer; memory behavior is unchanged no matter what you pass.
Driving train() directly writes only weights; write adapter_config.json yourself or downstream loads fail.
run() silently discards the training_callback you pass in; no metrics hooks ever fire.
DoRA dequantises the full base weight twice per forward, materialising dense layer-size matrices; QLoRA savings vanish.
DoRAEmbedding's guard tests QuantizedLinear, not QuantizedEmbedding; the meant error never fires, an unrelated one does.
Comparison table: DoRA runs on a quantized base but dequantises every step; don't use it where QLoRA memory matters.
--mlx-path must not already exist and there is no --force; delete the previous output directory first.
On M5/A19, affine gather_qmm silently corrupts MoE output (mlx#3856) for big row counts or K%64!=0; M1-M4 unaffected.
LoRA target keys use exact set membership; a glob or regex pattern silently selects zero layers.
get_total_parameters unpacks quantized weights in the denominator; the printed trainable fraction is misleadingly small.
Dropout fires only in training mode; train() and evaluate() toggle it, so know which mode your loop left the model in.
cosine_decay with decay_steps below iters bottoms the LR out early; the tail of training runs at the floor.
Warmup hands off at warmup_steps+1, not warmup_steps, and the cosine clock restarts there - an LR-path off-by-one.
Avoid --optimizer muon from the CLI; build MultiOptimizer in Python. Muon's doc page 404s though the class exists.
--iters counts micro-steps, not optimizer updates; with gradient accumulation you get fewer updates than you planned.
The trainer's printed peak memory excludes the buffer pool; the real footprint is active plus cache memory.
The memory-constrained path's loader accepts only .jsonl with a text field (or one alternate); other formats fail.
The length sort keys on len() of the raw record dict, a constant: batches mix short and long rows, causing random OOMs.
Resuming restores weights only; Adam moments and schedule position are silently reset to zero.
With --fine-tune-type full, lora_parameters is None and never read; a full config isn't interchangeable with LoRA's.
val_info['iteration'] is it-1 while train_info uses it; naive metric joins misalign validation by one step.
--batch-size is global and must be scaled by N; unscaled, each node quietly trains on batch/N.
JACCL recv spins forever on peer loss and the ring socket thread dies silently, wedging all ranks (#3910, #3862, #3830).
The before/after perplexity comparison lies three ways; perplexity on a tuned distribution always improves.
mlx_lm.perplexity takes no --adapter-path; fuse the adapter first to measure it this way.
lm-eval with --limit 200 across eight tasks is a smoke test, not a benchmark; don't publish those numbers.
Byte-identical greedy outputs mean the adapter never loaded: lora_b starts at zero, so unloaded equals the base model.
generate() returns None, not '', for empty output, and stream_generate(max_tokens=0) raises UnboundLocalError.
Doc bug: LORA.md's upload example passes --hf-path to mlx_lm.fuse; fuse.py declares eight flags and no such option.
Publish the adapter alongside the fused model; it's two orders of magnitude smaller and others can rebase it.
mlx_lm.server's own startup banner says it is not recommended for production; treat it as a dev tool.
This section is project READMEs only — nothing in it was cloned, run or measured; treat flag names as pointers to check.
